rewrites.0C24F464: The runway limits the peak hours until its relief arrives. Outside the Metro the product exists but is hard to reach without a car and uneven to stay in.
rewrites.5860C967: Seats pace growth at the peak; beyond the Metro the product exists but is hard to reach and to find.
rewrites.5A9FA478: Eleven of 27 international routes run above 80% load. The 2.5 million target requires about 1.2 million more inbound seats. The existing Cape Town Air Access partnership is scaled and re-termed to win frequency, larger aircraft and winter seats. Its route support carries resilience conditions, because the 2026 Gulf disruption showed that hubs in one region share risk.
rewrites.5AF3057A: The Western Cape received 64 cruise liner visits in 2025/26, down from 79 a season earlier. Cape Town's berth has room for 150 or more calls, so the berth is not the limit. Growth is set by the regional circuit that makes a Southern African season worth a ship's deployment and by shore capacity on call days, when passengers converge on flagship sites already full in season.
rewrites.45A65921: The gap in the middle of the accommodation market is a product question that differs by place, not a missing tier. Service, interpretation and language readiness thin out with distance from Cape Town. An accessible building is not yet an accessible trip.
rewrites.1F13D0E0: Boulders is near carrying capacity and Cableway queues reach three hours, so growth at the flagship nature sites must come from managing flows. Repairs come before new product. Receiving reserves pass a readiness assessment before visitors are steered to them.
rewrites.00C054C8: Goal 2 removes the mobility, infrastructure and product constraints that limit how many visitors the province can carry and where they can go. Conversion work in Goal 1 needs seats at the peak and it pays outside the Metro only if visitors can reach, find and stay in the product there (section 2.4).
rewrites.6D8135D3: The first constraint is the gateway at the peak. The 2.5 million target requires about 3.1 million inbound seats a year, about 1.2 million more than the year to November 2025. The growth model's 1.8 million figure marks 2025 capacity (section 2.4). The runway binds at peak hours. The international terminal upgrade at Cape Town International is due about 2032 and the relocated runway about 2033.[^294]
rewrites.27B637C3: Only the air entry needs more transport capacity. Cruise has room at the berth: it can take 150 or more calls a season and the province received 64 cruise liner visits in 2025/26. The flagship nature sites face a limit of a different kind, which calls for managing flows rather than adding volume (objective 12). The other three entries concern reach, product and experience. The entries also have an order. Seat retention at the gateway comes first; corridors, beds and regional information then decide where growth lands (section 2.4). Visas, air service agreements and the runway are national levers, which the province leads by escalation in Goal 3 (section 3.3.2).[^296]
rewrites.76DA3247: The first supply theme covers how visitors reach the province and move through it. Air access and cruise bring visitors in and internal mobility carries them beyond Cape Town.
rewrites.588A1E8F: Cape Town International is the province's only international airport, so the growth case runs through one gateway. Conversion comes first and seats pace it at the summer peak. The 2.5 million target requires about 3.1 million inbound seats a year, about 1.2 million more than the year to November 2025 (section 2.4).[^297]
rewrites.45C32911: Two limits bind at the peak. The first is commercial. Cape Town's best routes already run full. On the mature long-haul routes carriers are expected to raise fares rather than add services. The second is physical. A single main runway caps movements at about 30 an hour. The relocated runway that lifts the cap is due about 2033. ACSA's latest schedule is earlier, with the runway finished by December 2029, subject to contract award. The phasing in Chapter 4 assumes about 2033 and treats the earlier date as upside.[^298]
rewrites.32BC3E07: A third limit showed itself in 2026: reliance on hubs in one region. Emirates had 91% of its previous network operating at 30 September and carried 22% fewer passengers from April to September. ACSA's warning of 1 March included Cape Town (section 2.4). Alternatives are growing. The IAG winter schedule raises Heathrow to Cape Town from seven to 19 weekly flights.
rewrites.6B0B5833: Yet the province starts from strength. It added 17 mainline international routes between 2015 and 2025, more than any of eight peer airports. The task is to hold and enlarge those routes until the runway arrives and to have the next ones ready when it does.[^299]
rewrites.01E1DCFB: On air access the evidence describes a timing problem. The fares forecast covers the mature long-haul routes only and no fare data yet tests it. The five regional markets that also run above an 80% load factor are named for more capacity. The hub routes still have room, with Dubai at 72.3%, Addis Ababa at 71.9% and Doha at 65.2%. On those routes marketing can still fill seats.[^300]
rewrites.50E733F8: Relief also comes in the wrong order: the certain fix comes last and the earliest large option is the least certain. George doubles its capacity but flies domestic routes only. Cape Winelands stays a scenario until finance, licensing and carriers are shown. The province's aviation strategy identifies a possible upgrade that would let George handle international traffic. No airline is among the 16 organisations whose views this report draws on, so carriers' views on frequency and aircraft size are untested.[^301]
rewrites.023E93AE: New routes continue beside the full ones. Wesgro's plan expects 10 new routes, first-time scheduled international services, by FY30. Cape Town Air Access counts 33 route launches since 2015, about three a year. The 17 mainline routes added over the same decade make about 1.7 a year. Filling existing seats first still leaves room for new routes, because the runway binds at peak hours and new routes can land outside them. As reported in November 2025, Cape Town Air Access's short to medium term targets spanned Africa, Saudi Arabia, China, Hong Kong, India and Australia. The African and Saudi links fit before runway relief.[^303]
rewrites.35B4394D: The vehicle already exists. Cape Town Air Access has worked since 2015 as a partnership of six public bodies and private-sector partners, which fund and advise it. The six are the Western Cape Government, the City of Cape Town, Cape Town Tourism, Wesgro, SA Tourism and ACSA. The private partners named in 2026 are the V&A Waterfront and DHL. The action is to scale and re-term that partnership, not to design a fund. Five things are new. Support is sized to the seats the target requires (section 2.4). Winter seat retention becomes an explicit purpose. Budgets are ring-fenced by corridor. The partners make multi-year commitments. Hub-closure scenarios shape where support goes.[^304]
rewrites.43D086D4: The partners agree the new terms in 2027 and 2028, so they apply when the regional frequency cases are made from 2029. The India and China cases go to carriers from 2032, as runway capacity arrives (section 4.3). ACSA delivers the runway and terminals. Wesgro tracks them quarterly as the first risk. Air service agreements, the cap on US carriers and immigration processing sit with national government, so the province escalates them (section 3.3.2).
rewrites.5E7C6127: Model correlated hub-closure scenarios with flown-seat and itinerary data by hub; weight route work towards routings outside any one region
rewrites.0CAA8EE9: Chile shows the infrastructure half. A private concession funded about US$900 million of expansion at Santiago. International seats grew about 40% to 50% between 2013 and 2019 under open-skies agreements. The partnership is the province's to scale; open skies and private airport finance are national levers, carried in the escalation agenda (objective 19). The condition is the runway. If relief slips past about 2033, existing routes must carry growth for longer.[^306]
rewrites.33F3A8E0: Conditions on route money have precedent (Appendix A3). Queensland's Attracting Aviation Investment Fund matched A$100 million of government funding with A$100 million from airports and regional bodies and paid against delivered capacity. Scotland's independent evaluation of its route development fund used passenger surveys, an explicit counterfactual and carbon costs. Both are reported or evaluated results, not causal audits.
rewrites.5977D31E: **Initiative I6**, route development and seat retention through Cape Town Air Access (section 4.3). **Indicators** T1-01 international arrivals at impact level; T2-09 seats and routes and T2-10 seats added on full routes at outcome level, both read against the seats the target requires. T3-39, hub-closure scenarios completed, measures the output (section 5.2).
rewrites.5CE30301: The Western Cape received 64 cruise liner visits in 2025/26, down from 79 a season earlier. Cape Town's berth has room for 150 or more calls, so the berth is not the limit. Growth is set by the regional circuit that makes a Southern African season worth a ship's deployment and by shore capacity on call days, when passengers converge on flagship sites already full in season.
rewrites.21B4F264: Cruise has room to grow at the berth Cape Town already has. The equipped berth can take 150 or more calls a season; it handled 83 in 2024/25 and the province received 64 cruise liner visits in 2025/26. The 2025/26 season brought R1.47 billion of spending and added R1.35 billion to provincial GDP-R, against about R1.79 billion after displacement a season earlier. The berth is not what limits growth.[^307]
rewrites.2FE9D7BA: The regional circuit decides whether ships come. A line commits a ship to Southern Africa for a season only when the whole itinerary works. Cape Town is the homeport, with calls east towards the Indian Ocean islands and west towards Angola and St Helena (section 2.4). The province holds one equipped port in that circuit. Mossel Bay and Saldanha Bay can extend it east and west. Stakeholders name home porting and expedition vessels as the segments that bring longer stays and higher local spend.[^309]
rewrites.3905D2E9: Shore capacity decides what a call is worth (section 2.4). On call days passengers converge on flagship sites that are already full in season and the terminal queues about ten coaches at a time. The berth itself takes ships of up to 300m, the South-Easter delays berthing and there is no shore power. Port capital goes to freight: Saldanha's R4 billion iron-ore expansion and Cape Town's container expansion add no cruise capacity.[^310]
rewrites.3DD12599: Cape Town's berth has room and value grows with international passengers; the regional circuit and call-day shore capacity set growth; port capital is going to freight.
rewrites.2B09CF41: Source: Cruise Economic Contribution Study 2024/25, Oct 2025 (Cruise Study; GDP-R after displacement); Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025 (Diag); Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026 (IR); Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026 (SIR); Wesgro, Why Cruise to Cape Town & the Western Cape, Oct 2026 (Prospectus); City of Cape Town media release, 11 Mar 2025 (City). For the same season the Cruise Economic Contribution Study counts 79 vessel visits and 127,128 passengers; the Diagnostic 79 and 127,178; the Infrastructure Report 83 calls. The 2025/26 figures are the prospectus's headline results from Cruise Cape Town's 2025/26 economic study, which is not in hand. Mossel Bay's 27 a season is its own figure; section 2.4 sets out the Mossel Bay counts.
rewrites.3260C68F: The evidence sets a clear stance: protect Cape Town, back Mossel Bay now and watch Saldanha Bay. Mossel Bay handled 21 calls in 2024/25, opened a new passenger facility in November 2025 and expected about 23 calls in 2025/26. Wesgro counts 13 cruise liner visits across Mossel Bay, Hermanus and Saldanha Bay for that season (section 2.4). Ships anchor and tender at Mossel Bay. Only small and mid-sized ships call. Saldanha Bay has no passenger facility. The regional ports work as day stops rather than home ports, so they spread spend rather than multiply the passenger total.[^311]
rewrites.43E98016: The actions match the constraint. The berth has headroom; what limits growth is the circuit that brings a ship for a season and the shore capacity that receives its passengers. A circuit compact gives lines a full itinerary. Shore programmes give passengers more to buy beyond the flagships. Regional day stops spread that spend along the coast.[^313]
rewrites.6FE3B676: The best precedent is local. On its own count, Mossel Bay's calls rose from four before COVID-19 to 27 a season, supported by closer coordination and better excursion packaging. The town credits its partnership with Wesgro. No benchmark destination offers a cruise precedent, so the case rests on Mossel Bay. The condition is that ship deployments hold. Growth to 2024/25 leaned on Red Sea reroutes and their reversal is the main risk. Visits fell from 79 to 64 in 2025/26.[^314]
rewrites.72BE0E7F: The problem is reach, not capacity. Even in the Metro no rail line reaches the airport. Safety perceptions and limited visitor wayfinding hold back Metrorail's tourism potential. In April 2025 the Department of Mobility reported that no mass public transport served the airport and that the MyCiTi airport service had been suspended since 2022. Stakeholders call weak public transport, congestion and unreliable last-mile access structural barriers to visitor movement.[^316]
rewrites.003F173A: No single body owns the visitor's journey. The Department of Mobility notes that mobility responsibilities are split across three tiers of government and argues the case for a dedicated transport authority.[^317]
rewrites.19CA0FDB: The MyCiTi airport service is suspended and ACSA's own pages conflict on where e-hailing pickup sits
rewrites.338BF6F1: The evidence shows transport assets that exist but are not run for visitors. The Southern Line runs from Cape Town through Muizenberg and Kalk Bay to Fish Hoek as a low-cost scenic corridor, with a Simon's Town section whose regular service PRASA has yet to confirm. Trains do not normally run on Sundays or public holidays, Boulders needs a transfer from Simon's Town station and the line's visitor branding dates to 2007. The gaps between towns are services rather than roads. The Garden Route has no inter-town shuttle despite obvious demand. Hermanus, Stanford, Elim and Agulhas have no public tourism transport between them.[^318]
rewrites.564C5912: This objective is also a conversion measure. Reluctance to self-drive is one of the six barriers between interest and a visit (section 2.1). A trip sold with its transfers included reaches the visitor who would otherwise stay in the city or not come.
rewrites.254C660F: Wesgro does not build transport. It makes existing transport usable for visitors and gathers the demand that makes shuttles pay. The Department of Mobility holds the transport lever and Wesgro's Tourism unit convenes the work. Wesgro pilots shuttle aggregation and transfers sold inside itineraries in 2027 and 2028. Shuttle products run from 2029. The April 2025 draft land transport framework targets MyCiTi Phase 2A to Khayelitsha and Mitchells Plain for 2027, which would bring township product within reach sooner. The Department of Mobility's draft Tourism Transport Strategy adds the airport leg and touring-route signage, so Wesgro also sells airport transfers inside itineraries.[^320]
rewrites.60BC5846: Funded service specifications come first. They cover the airport link and regional services. They are written for visitors without cars. The MyCiTi grant and the suspended airport service take priority over rail branding. Phase 2A is counted only once its funding is confirmed. Airport pickup information is harmonised across ACSA, the City and operators. The Southern Line product proceeds only on a PRASA-signed timetable with security and disruption obligations. Rapid rail to George waits for an appraisal of cheaper options. The last mile to Cape Point comes later in the period (section 4.3). On the George bus the national ask narrows to the written technical or regulatory reason for refusing direct bank-card tapping, from the Department of Transport and the payment provider. Airport-corridor safety costs sit once, in I17.
rewrites.2B6D9988: Write funded service specifications for the airport link and regional services, including for visitors without cars; secure MyCiTi funding beyond the grant that ends in 2027/28
rewrites.33ADB83A: Appraise cheaper options before any Cape Town to George rapid rail decision and extend the George public transport model
rewrites.4010B223: Obtain from the Department of Transport and the payment provider the written technical or regulatory reason for refusing direct bank-card tapping on the George bus; fund passenger rail beyond the Metro
rewrites.43385A93: The mechanism is aggregation. A shuttle pays only at volume. Pooled bookings across operators, sold inside a multi-day itinerary, turn scattered requests into a load that can run. The Southern Line needs no new track to become a product, but it does need a timetable PRASA will sign and security a visitor can rely on. Each step widens the market to visitors without a car, the market that limited public transport now narrows.[^321]
rewrites.63F7865A: None of the six benchmark destinations carries an internal mobility lever with figures. Medellín shows the principle at city scale. A cable-car line carrying about 35,000 passengers a day and six outdoor escalators, built for Comuna 13's residents, became part of the visit. The area drew 1.98 million visitors in 2025, 52% of them international. The Cape Winelands shows it at home: its heritage tram, built to connect wine estates, solves the drink-and-drive barrier. The condition is shared ownership and an early capacity limit. The three tiers must run the visitor's journey as one and trains must be safe enough to sell. Visitor caps must also come before the crowds, which in Comuna 13 they did not.[^322]
rewrites.14DEC95D: **Initiative I8**, corridor mobility (section 4.3). **Indicators** T1-06 share of arrivals and spend outside the Metro at impact level and T2-12 accessibility score by district and T2-13 corridor transfer products at outcome level (section 5.2).
rewrites.75EAA82D: The growth case needs visitors to travel beyond the Cape Peninsula, stay longer and spend in more places. The province has the assets to support that. Of 50,332 mapped tourism assets, the Cape Metro holds 40.3% and the five other districts the rest. The West Coast's natural assets rate close to the Metro's for attractiveness and the Central Karoo holds the province's most unique niche assets.[^323]
rewrites.4642BC36: Yet both score lowest on readiness and the product around the assets is unfinished (section 2.4). Eleven of 16 organisations engaged see the offer as concentrated around Cape Town and a narrow set of icons. The Department of Economic Development adds that destination development has focused more on managing barriers than on building product outside the Cape Peninsula.[^324]
rewrites.7FCB7382: An attraction without an online ticket is not always unsold. Walk-in entry and local permits can be workable access models. The test is whether the visitor can plan and complete the trip and whether the operator loses profitable sales.
rewrites.6A9FCD51: The first product is the regional add-on. A two-to-three-night extension to a Cape Town stay, with the transfer included, is the simplest regional product to sell and the one the extension strategy in objective 5 needs. The Cape Winelands, the Whale Coast and the Garden Route can each supply one from existing product. Wesgro designs the add-ons in 2027.
rewrites.58974F2B: The City is a natural partner. Its framework for 2019 to 2024 proposed a Cape Town+ offer linking the city with the surrounding regions. Stellenbosch and George can anchor regional business events, which gives the Convention Bureau a part to play. The capital sits with others. Accommodation investors and municipalities add beds and service depth in secondary towns later in the period (objective 15). SANParks carries the precinct projects. Rural broadband sits with national government (objective 3).[^329]
rewrites.0CA81129: The actions supply what the assets lack: a guide, a bed and a booking route. Packaging turns scattered assets into a trip a visitor can buy. A multi-day itinerary gives a reason to stay outside the Metro. The Overberg shows both the pull and the limit. Its whale-watching anchor sustains operator confidence despite flat accessibility, yet De Hoop still lacks accommodation investment and year-round product is unfunded.[^330]
rewrites.20032C82: Accommodation outside the Metro has gaps in the middle of the market that differ by place. Service, interpretation, language and access readiness thin out with distance from Cape Town.
rewrites.0F8594F0: The growth case needs visitors the current offer serves poorly. The gap in the middle of the accommodation market is a product question, not a province-wide absence. In the Cape Winelands, mid-market stock is effectively absent outside Stellenbosch and a luxury-skewed product mix excludes mid-market and family segments. The Garden Route is described as short of quality-graded hotels that anchor midweek, conference or business travel, yet George already has a branded, conference-capable hotel of 109 rooms. What is missing is a configuration, price point, location or capacity and it differs by place.[^332]
rewrites.45E39F83: Access and information are part of the experience. A graded building is not an accessible trip: the transfer, the room, the attraction and the information must work end to end. TGCSA guidance on universal access already exists. Halal and vegetarian claims must match what is delivered. Guide registration is under strain, with application growth, overtime and burnout recorded in DEDAT's 2026/27 plan. Short-term rentals supply much of the self-catering stock visitors already favour, yet no count sets them beside hotels and guesthouses (section 2.4).
rewrites.2F4AE489: Two measures are missing. No source counts rooms or beds by district and type, short-term rentals included. None gives a visitor satisfaction score.
rewrites.6FF43410: The quality charter comes first, because it sets the standard the other actions aim at. DEDAT leads it with Wesgro's Tourism unit. It is a province-wide framework that aligns all tourism stakeholders under consistent benchmarks, phased by district, with support for SMMEs to comply. It works as a supported condition for discretionary public promotion, not as a new badge: operators who meet it, with help where they need it, are the ones public campaigns carry. Design runs through 2027 and 2028. The district phases start in 2029 (section 4.3).[^336]
rewrites.067E2A06: The accommodation question becomes a destination-and-product test, run with I14 (objective 15). It asks which configuration, price point, location or capacity is missing in each place and whether better use of existing stock answers it. An accommodation audit counts hotel, guesthouse and short-term rental stock separately by district. The arrival gate sits outside the province's reach: Home Affairs and ACSA hold immigration processing and peak-hour throughput at Cape Town International, so the province presses them.
rewrites.7D7B9B9D: Improve immigration processing and peak-hour throughput at Cape Town International and deliver the terminal relief due about 2032
rewrites.7F1D6AF0: A visible standard solves a problem of trust. A visitor booking a guesthouse on Route 62 cannot judge its service from abroad; certification shown on the booking platform can. The same standard gives small operators a clear target and a route to support. It lets the province sell product outside the core with confidence.
rewrites.304B8DAF: The flagship nature sites carry the province's brand. Table Mountain, Robben Island and Kirstenbosch form the only globally branded landmark cluster. The Metro holds five of the province's six highest-volume attractions. In season they run full (section 2.4). Peak queues at the Cableway of up to three hours detract from the visitor experience.[^338]
rewrites.5D8745BE: More volume at these sites is the wrong aim. The Department of Economic Development wants further growth directed to under-visited parts of the province rather than constrained flagships. Yet the flagships congest at the peak while the overflow reserves remain under-marketed. Stony Point, a penguin colony in the Overberg, is the candidate alternative to Boulders at the peak and its visitors rose 28% over the festive season (section 2.4). Yet its R45 entry and opening hours establish neither spare ecological capacity nor readiness for coaches, so it must pass its own readiness assessment first.[^339]
rewrites.68BE9AC6: Maintenance is the first call on that revenue. CapeNature's audited 2025/26 accounts show ecotourism revenue of R82.038 million, against a restated R77.171 million the year before, repairs of R16.058 million and government grants of R331.562 million. Its 2026/27 Ecotourism and Access budget is R132.542 million, including R35.599 million for buildings. Floods in May 2026 damaged roads, trails and buildings. By June 85% of reserves reported some damage. The reserves expected to take the overflow therefore need repair before they need marketing.
rewrites.1C711A46: CapeNature's ecotourism income pays for alien clearing, fire response and species protection; public funding alone will not suffice
rewrites.217C9657: From 1 November 2026 Boulders costs R57 for South African adults and R282 for international adults; Cape Point R592 for international adults; Stony Point charges R45
rewrites.74D40ADA: Maintenance comes before new product. CapeNature and the site operators compile a costed condition register. Repairs of verified assets come first. Two flow pilots move into the first phase: Boulders and one other constrained site, in the summer of 2027/28 at the earliest. Each protects walk-up access and resident access and carries a stop rule.
rewrites.085F3897: The site operators hold the flow tools, from digital flow management to tiered pricing. The pilots test them first. From 2029 the operators extend what works at the Cableway and Boulders, where mandates allow. Later in the period CapeNature makes reserve product climate-resilient. SANParks carries the national step: a visitor management plan for Table Mountain National Park and Boulders, agreed with the City and the operators.[^343]
rewrites.3B9051A2: Market receiving reserves (Stony Point included) and the Southern Line towns only once each passes its own readiness assessment, as alternatives to peak-hour visits at Boulders and the Cableway
rewrites.3622F1AF: Compile a costed condition register for reserve and attraction assets; repair verified assets before adding new product
rewrites.2F6A9C0A: Flow management protects the visit and the revenue together. Digital flow tools and tiered pricing spread arrivals across the day and the season. A site then serves its visitors without a three-hour queue and earns more at the peak. Marketing the alternatives at the point of booking sends the overflow to reserves that are ready for it and their income pays for conservation there.
rewrites.27F0E927: New Zealand uses land-use controls and premium curation on the principle that capacity discipline protects long-term pricing power. Kenya treats conservation as national economic infrastructure, with tourism-funded conservation financing and community conservancies that sustain demand and environmental integrity. The City already runs the model at small scale. Since August 2025 Witzands permits have been capped by day and 80% are pre-booked online. The condition is the operators. They must share their counts. Their mandates must allow pricing: CapeNature's statutory affordability mandate has kept its prices conservative and CapeNature is now moving towards tiered pricing.[^344]
